doc_summary: The paper argues that LLM jailbreak and prompt-injection defenses must be evaluated against strong, adaptive attackers (gradient, RL, search, and human red-teaming) rather than static attack sets or weak generic optimizers, and breaks 12 defenses with >90% ASR for most. It stresses that evaluations should fail to break a defense only after trying as hard as possible, and that automated scorers and static benchmarks give misleading evidence.

items.claim: prefers evaluations against adaptive, resource-rich adversaries over static fixed test sets because static sets overfit and real attacks are out of distribution, giving a false sense of security.
items.quote: Second, because adversarial tasks are inherently open-ended, real attacks will inevitably be out of distribution, so success on static evaluations provides only a false sense of security.

items.claim: prefers a negative-result standard of 'tried as hard as possible and still failed' over claiming robustness from empirical success, because evaluations can only fail to prove a thing is broken.
items.quote: empirical evaluations cannot prove that a defense is robust; all it can (and should) do is fail to prove that the defense is broken! A defense evaluation should try as hard as possible to break the defense and ultimately fail.

items.claim: Distrusts near-zero attack success rates reported on public benchmarks, treating them as a sign of weak evaluation rather than a strong system.
items.quote: Indeed, defenses that merely report near-zero attack success rates on public benchmarks are often among the easiest to break once novel attacks are attempted.

items.claim: Distrusts automated model-based graders because they are themselves ML models that can be gamed or reward-hacked, so scoring needs manual checking.
items.quote: these safety classifiers are themselves machine learning models and are consequently susceptible to adversarial examples and reward-hacking behaviors

items.claim: Manually verifies successful attacks to ensure they are not exploiting weaknesses in the scoring mechanism before counting them as evidence.
items.quote: We manually verified all attacks to ensure they were not exploiting weaknesses in our scoring mechanism.

items.claim: prefers including human red-teamers alongside automated attacks because humans succeeded in every case even with limited information, where automated search succeeded only part of the time.
items.quote: human red-teaming succeeds in all the cases we evaluated, even when the participants have only limited information and feedback from the target system. On a selected subset of scenarios and defenses, the search attack succeeds 69% of the time

items.claim: prefers tailoring attacks to the specific defense design (assuming the attacker knows the system) over generic off-the-shelf attacks, because evaluation should reflect the intrinsic strength of the system rather than attacker limitations.
items.quote: the adversary is assumed to know the system design and to possess sufficient computational power, so that the evaluation reflects the intrinsic strength of the defense rather than limitations of the attacker.

items.claim: Tests mechanisms that depend on hidden information by simulating an attacker with perfect knowledge of the defense, which reveals conditional strategies a naive attacker would only find by chance.
items.quote: When we simulate a stronger adversary with perfect knowledge of the MELON paper and implementation, the mutator quickly discovers a “conditional” strategy

items.claim: Treats detection-based defenses as weak when attacks look benign out of context, since flagging them would raise false positives; benign-looking triggers are hard to distinguish from normal inputs.
items.quote: Many successful triggers, including the example below, are not obviously harmful or show clear intention to overwrite the user instruction. Hence, the detectors cannot flag such triggers as unsafe, especially out of context

items.claim: Calls for more robust and efficient adaptive evaluation procedures, and for making defenses easy for humans to probe.
items.quote: we encourage the community to continue developing more robust and efficient adaptive evaluation procedures.
